# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

FACTS.md:93
- F-88 **The compiled checker reads what a trait or object provides by the traits chapter's inheritance, and checks an overriding declaration's return type against the one it overrides.** A type provides its own methods and its immediate supertypes', less those that an own declaration overrides or repeats in its parameter types. # Climb batch 35: the judge's ruling on the red gate

Decision: **repair**, on the merged tree. No rung is dropped. The cause is not established by reading, so the repair's first steps are a diagnosis by run, which the judge's role does not make; the steps and the rule for each outcome are below.

## What is red

One suite: `fast-onelibrary/OneLibraryJUTest`, 40 tests, 9 failures (`tmp/gate-batch-35/out/summary.txt:59`; the last landed summary, `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-34b/gate/summary.txt:59`, has 40 and 0). The 9 are the suite's run tests. Each dies as the one library's class initialises, from `grep -n -A16 "run .*OneLibraryVarargsCount" tmp/gate-batch-35/testFast.txt`:

    fortress/FortressLibrary$QQ$DefaultTraitMethods.isFinite(Lfortress/FortressLibrary$QQ;)...FBoolean; @1: invokestatic
    Type 'fortress/FortressLibrary$QQ' (current frame, stack[0]) is not assignable to 'fortress/FortressLibrary$Ratio'
    0000000: 2ab8 0064 c000 66b2 0069 59c7 0007 57b8

The bytes are `aload_0; invokestatic #100; checkcast #102; ...`: the first call of the body of `getter isFinite(): Boolean = (denominator(self) =/= 0)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:641`) is compiled as a static call whose parameter is the object `Ratio`, where the argument's static type is the trait `QQ`. `QQ` declares `denominator(self): ZZ` abstract (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:643`) and `Ratio` implements it (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:729`). The library compiled cold in the suite (`tmp/gate-batch-35/testFast.txt:3072`, `FortressLibrary  OK (time = 109117ms)`), so the bytes are the merged compiler's. Every other gate step is clean.

## The gate's claims

Right:

- The suite is red and was green at the last landing (citations above), and no test or library file of the suite changed in the batch: `git diff --stat 13f4fdea75 HEAD -- ProjectFortress/one_library_tests Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` prints nothing.
- The compiled path's sources that the batch changed are `OverloadSet.java` (S), `CodeGen.java`, `STypesUtil.scala` and `OverloadingChecker.scala` (O). `DesugarerVisitor.java` (W) is walk's alone: its only user is `interpreter/env/CUWrapper.java`. `ExprFactory.java` (R) changes `makeFloatLiteralExpr` only (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nodes_util/ExprFactory.java:1630-1640`). `BaseTask.java` (A) is run time and cannot change a call site's descriptor.
- It did not establish which rung caused it.

Not supported by the code: that rung O's skip and bridges or rung S's `argumentLocal` are the cause by their logic. Read against the one library, each is inert at this call site:

- O. No declaration of the one library has the modifier: `grep -rnw override Library/*.fs? ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/*.fs?` finds comments only. So `STypesUtil.overriddenNotProvided` returns its empty list at `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1805`, the map `overriddenHere` is empty at both sites of `CodeGen.java` (the skip in the method-chaining loop, `:1113-1115`, and the lookup `overriddenHere.get(super_func)`, `:1476`), `overrideBridges` loops over nothing, and `checkOverridesSomething` (`OverloadingChecker.scala:763-789`) only raises an error and its filter starts at `o.mods.isOverride`. The functions O calls before the early return (`allMethods`, `gatherMethods`, `declaredMethods`, `STypesUtil.scala:1623-1672, 1858-1896`) build new relations and write nothing shared.
- S. `argumentLocal` returns `j + first`, the base's expression, except in `ForTraitOrObject` where `j < selfIndex` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java:2361-2363, 2503-2508`), and it is called only inside a dispatch method's body (`:1538, :1876`). The failing instruction is in `isFinite`'s own body, a call site, not a dispatch method; and `denominator`'s self is first.

## The likely cause, a hypothesis

FACTS **F-354** ("Two compiles of one source by different builds of the compiler need not give the same bytes ... a result that depends on the order can come and go between builds") and ledger row 996 (the code generator's order follows the JVM's identity hashes; "No site traced") describe this failure's kind. O's new code runs for every trait and object of every compile, in the checker and in the code generator, and hashes tuples that hold objects hashed by identity before it returns empty; that moves the identity hashes of everything made after it on that thread, and so the iteration order of every identity-hashed set later in the compile. FACTS **F-232** names such objects: "`DeclaredFunction`s, entries of the checker's index and not nodes, still hash by identity". If the choice of the overloading at which a call of `denominator(self)` is compiled depends on such an order, where an abstract functional method and its implementation in the one comprised object are both candidates, this batch's build can take the other branch with no line of the batch at fault. This is a hypothesis: nothing was run for it. Steps 1 to 3 test it.

## What the right behaviour is

The call's argument has static type `QQ`. A declaration is applicable to a named functional call by the static types of the call's arguments (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:36-44`, and its section on applicability; `Specification/basic/functions.tex:224-232`), and `Ratio`'s `denominator(self)` takes a `Ratio`, which `QQ` is not below. So the call is compiled at an arrow whose parameter is `QQ` or above, and the run-time dispatch reaches `Ratio`'s declaration. A call site whose descriptor takes `Ratio` is a defect of the compiler whatever order produced it. The 9 tests are right as written and change no line.

## Instructions for the repair

Work in `/home/user/fortress`, on main, as the `fortress-repo` skill says (private caches for every compile; long commands in the background; the base's code only through `/home/user/fortress-base42/explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh` with a private caches folder). Scratch goes under `tmp/repair-gate/`.

1. Reproduce outside the suite. With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` and a private caches folder, compile the one library's fourteen components and `ProjectFortress/one_library_tests/OneLibraryRunHello.fss` on the merged tree, in the way `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/tests-running.md:119` gives (`OneLibraryComponents.test` first), keep the jars, and run it: expect the `VerifyError` of `tmp/gate-batch-35/testFast.txt:3422-3438`. From the `FortressLibrary` jar, `javap -c -p` the class `fortress/FortressLibrary$QQ$DefaultTraitMethods` and record the owner, name and descriptor of the `invokestatic` at offset 1 of `isFinite`.
2. The same compile with the base's code (`old-fortress.sh`, its own private caches), and the same `javap` line. Record both lines in the repair's report. The base's line is the call the merged tree must make again, or its equal.
3. Test the order. Compile the base's code once more with `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx... -Xss32m -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:hashCode=0"` (the flag of row 996; `bin/fortress:28-32` reads `JAVA_FLAGS`, so keep the memory flags the skill gives), and the merged code with the same flag. If the base's code under the flag makes the `Ratio` call, or the merged code under it makes the base's call, the choice depends on identity hashes: go to step 4. If all four agree with their own build whatever the flag, the cause is a rung's logic: in a scratch worktree off the merged tree, revert `d56eb8a882`'s three source files (O) and repeat step 1; if still red, restore them and revert `1db0e878c8`'s `OverloadSet.java` (S). Go to step 5 with the rung found.
4. Order-dependent choice (the expected case). Trace where the `FnRef` of `denominator` at `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:641` gets the names and the overloading type that `CodeGen.forFnRef` compiles it at (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:4361-4400, 4527-4545, 4585-4650`; the rewriting at `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadRewriteVisitor.java:109, 161`; the checker's set of a component's functions, which drops an abstract functional method that a subtype implements, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:119-163`). Find the iteration over an identity-hashed collection that picks between `QQ`'s declaration and `Ratio`'s, and make the choice by the rule above: the declarations applicable to the arguments' static types, the most specific of those, never one that is not applicable; where a collection's order still reaches the output, order it by a key that does not depend on identity (the declaration's span, as the tree's other sorts do). Do not revert or reshape O or S to move the hashes back: that hides the defect, and F-354 says it would return with the next change of the compiler.
5. A rung's logic (only if step 3 found one). Repair inside that rung's own members, keeping its tests green: for O the two `overriddenHere` sites and `overrideBridges` in `CodeGen.java` and `STypesUtil.overriddenNotProvided`; for S `ForTraitOrObject.argumentLocal`. The rung's approach stands unless the repair cannot keep both its tests and the 9; in that case stop and report to the judge with the `javap` lines, and change nothing.
6. Test first. The 9 run tests fail on the merged tree and are the repair's failing tests. Add one test of the compiler's own track if step 4's site can be reached without the one library: under `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/`, a trait that comprises one object, declares an abstract functional method `f(self)` and a concrete getter whose body calls `f(self)`, the object implementing `f`; `compile` and `run`, asserting the getter's value; one comment line saying what it checks. If it does not fail before the fix under either hash mode, do not add it, and say so in the report.
7. Verify, after the last change of code: `ant testOneLibrary` (40 tests, 0 failures); the batch's compiled tests of S and O through the tree's `junit.sh` (`FunctionalMethodOverloadSelfLast`, `FunctionalMethodCoverSelfSecond`, `FunctionalMethodSelfSecondReceiverTested`, `FunctionalMethodMeetNarrowedSelfNotFirst`, `OverrideModifierCodeGeneration`, and the `XXXOverride*` tests of `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/`); and step 1's program under both hash modes, both printing `Hello, one library`. #!/bin/bash
# junit.sh <label> <dir-of-tests> <Name.test>... : the gather of climb batch N runs each .test through the
# harness in the main tree (fortress junit, the compiled test harness, as climb batch 6.5's gather ran its pair),
# in the order given, so that a link test runs before its XXX run test. Each named component's cache entries are
# removed before the list and after it. First line: the machine line (protocol.md, principle 2).
# ONE_JVM=1 (added 2026-09-29 for the repair on the merged tree, coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md, "A repair
# of tests and records only"): the whole list in one fortress junit run, one JVM, as the gate's track runs them
# together; Shell junit hands the list to FileTests.suiteFromListOfFiles (Shell.java:1086), which puts its
# compile and link tests before its run tests (FileTests.java:997-1004), so a link test still runs first.
# The environment is env.sh's, set here without sourcing it, since env.sh also removes parser directories in
# /tmp. The tree is the one this script is in. FORTRESS_THREADS=4 is the pin of build.xml's fastTrack macro,
# which runs the gate's compiled tracks. The JVMs keep their temporary files, parser directories among them,
# in the tree's tmp/.
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64
export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH"
export FORTRESS_HOME="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../../.." && pwd)"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
export FORTRESS_THREADS=4
mkdir -p "$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp"
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp"
FH=$FORTRESS_HOME; L=${1:?label}; D=$(cd "${2:?dir}" && pwd); shift 2
cd "$FH/ProjectFortress"
CP=$(../bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
echo "# junit.sh $L $(date -u +%FT%TZ); nproc $(nproc); $(grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //'); $(grep -m1 'cpu MHz' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //') MHz; load at start $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | head -1); FORTRESS_THREADS=$FORTRESS_THREADS; tree $(git -C $FH rev-parse --short HEAD)$(git -C $FH diff --quiet HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library || echo ' with the next rung applied, not yet committed'); tests from $D"
clean () { for t in "$@"; do n=$(sed -n 's/^tests=//p' "$D/$t" | head -1); [ -n "$n" ] && find ../default_repository/caches -name "*$n*" -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null; done; }
clean "$@"
if [ -n "${ONE_JVM:-}" ]; then
  files=(); for t in "$@"; do files+=("$D/$t"); done
  echo "########## [$L] fortress junit, one JVM: $*"
  java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell junit "${files[@]}" 2>&1 | sed "s#$FH/##g" | grep -v '^\s*at ' | cut -c1-240
  echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
else
for t in "$@"; do
  echo "########## [$L] fortress junit $t"
  java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell junit "$D/$t" 2>&1 | sed "s#$FH/##g" | grep -v '^\s*at ' | cut -c1-240
  echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
done
fi
clean "$@"

#!/bin/bash
# old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...
#
# Runs the old code, the base's: bin/fortress of the batch's one base build, with FORTRESS_HOME set to the
# base build and FORTRESS_CACHES to a private caches folder. If the folder does not exist yet, it is first
# made as a copy of the base build's default_repository/caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). The paths in those caches
# are the base build's own, so nothing is translated, and no worktree is made.
#
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss    the compiled path: compile ...
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P            ... then run
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss            walk
#
# Every cache a run writes goes to the private folder: every cache directory and the logs are under
# fortress.caches (repository/ProjectProperties.java:283-299), which FORTRESS_CACHES sets, and
# bin/fortress_classpath and bin/run_classpath put FORTRESS_CACHES/bytecode_cache on the class path.
# Under the base build a run reads the build, the library sources and default_repository/configuration, and
# writes nothing that stays: the parser writes its error logs beside each file it parses from source and
# deletes them (compiler/Parser.java:349-367), so a compile of a program that exports Executable creates and
# deletes two empty, gitignored logs beside Library/Executable.fsi. Two runs at once may share those two
# names; that is harmless, because the base's library parses without errors, so both logs stay empty and
# a log removed by the other run reads as empty (Parser.java:373-377). Measured in
# explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md, section 6.
#
# Keep the private folder and your programs outside the base build (the program's own logs go beside it).
# Refuses (exit 2) a base build that is not built, and a private folder inside the base build.
set -euo pipefail
USAGE='usage: old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...'
BASE=$(realpath "${1:?$USAGE}")
PRIV_ARG=${2:?$USAGE}
shift 2
[ -x "$BASE/bin/fortress" ] && [ -e "$BASE/ProjectFortress/build/com/sun/fortress/Shell.class" ] \
  && [ -e "$BASE/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar" ] \
  || { echo "old-fortress: $BASE is not a built tree" >&2 ; exit 2 ; }
PRIV=$(realpath -m "$PRIV_ARG")
case "$PRIV/" in "$BASE"/*) echo "old-fortress: $PRIV is inside the base build $BASE" >&2 ; exit 2 ;; esac
if [ ! -d "$PRIV" ]; then
    mkdir -p "$(dirname "$PRIV")"
    PART="$PRIV.part.$$"
    cp -a "$BASE/default_repository/caches" "$PART"
    mv -T "$PART" "$PRIV" 2>/dev/null || rm -rf "$PART"     # another run made it first: use that one
fi
FORTRESS_HOME="$BASE" FORTRESS_CACHES="$PRIV" exec "$BASE/bin/fortress" "$@"

        r = nl MOD dl
        if r=0 then (q,1)
        else

    coerce(x: ZZ32) = Ratio(x, 1)

    getter zero(): QQ = Ratio(0, 1)
    getter one(): QQ = Ratio(1, 1)
    getter isNaN(): Boolean
    getter isInfinite(): Boolean
    getter isNumber(): Boolean = NOT self.isNaN
    getter isFinite(): Boolean = (denominator(self) =/= 0)

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## Landed semantics

FACTS.md:283
- F-377 **The compiled code casts `self` where the checker reads it as a listed type or as the self-type parameter.** `CodeGen.castToTypeBelow` casts a value that has self's type (the checker's `TraitSelfType` with a non-empty list: a trait whose `comprises` clause lists types, or a trait with a self-type parameter) to a declared trait type or type variable strictly below its trait. It casts at the argument of a call with one argument (a call with several arguments casts each already), at a typed binding and an assignment, at a method's returned value, at each arm of a conditional or a `case` expression, at the conditional's type, and at a function expression's and a local function's result, also where the value is a typecase whose arms each have self's type. So `den(self)` for `den(r: R)` in `trait Q comprises { R }`, `twin(self): S = self` and `mx(self, other: T): T = if lt(other, self) then self else other end` in a self-typed trait verify and run (rows 991, 695, 1050 and 1051, fixed), as the one library's `QQ comprises { Ratio }` and `StandardTotalOrder`'s `MIN` and `MAX` need. A conditional or typecase whose arms are pairs that hold `self`, `MINMAX`'s shape, verifies and runs with no cast, since the declared tuple type is a JVM interface and the caller converts the result; a typecase whose arms are all `self` has a one-element union, which is cast. Only `self` gets the reading: the checker refuses a variable declared at the trait where a listed type is expected. A typecase with `self` in one arm and another value in the other gets no cast (row 1070), and a trait that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable gets none (row 307). An assignment from outside an object to its `var` field, of a value whose static type is a strict subtype of the field's type, fails at run time, `NoSuchMethodError`, also for `c.r := self` at a listed type (row 1053). No cast is added where the value's type is a subtype of the declared type by `extends`. Two casts are added where the verifier, which checks no interface type, needs none: at a declared trait type strictly below self's trait, a planner's default; and at an arm that is `self` where the conditional stands at a trait type, as `atQ(c: Boolean): Q = if c then self else R(0, 0) end` gains `checkcast R`, a worker's choice beyond the plan. The curator has decided neither. Tests: `compiler_tests/ComprisesValueAtListedTypeCompiled`, `ComprisesValueAtConditionalArmRun`, `ComprisesValueFromClosureRun`, `SelfTypeReturnSelfRu

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:61
- P-146 **In a self-typed trait, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as also being the implementing type.** A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`, such as `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`. In its method bodies, `self` has the type `C[\X\] & X`. The method signatures keep the plain trait type. Only the overloading check's exclusion test reads `self` in a signature as `C[\X\] & X` (P-157). The checker refuses a type that extends such a trait at another type, since an extender must be a subtype of the static argument that it gives: `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, because `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. Scala has the same rule for self types. The library's text gains no self type and no `comprises` clause, and walk is unchanged. The rule accepts every self-typed method body of the library except `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead. Why: the checker reads the library as the team wrote it, as P-44 does for the closure of `AnyIntegral`, by one rule that peer languages share. F-225 states the rule as built.

(* A value typed by a trait stands, compiled, where a type that the trait's comprises clause lists is expected: as an argument of a function, a method and a constructor, as a returned value, at a typed binding and at an assignment. *)
component ComprisesValueAtListedTypeCompiled
export Executable

trait Q comprises { R }
    getter fin(): Boolean = (den(self) > 0)
    numBy(t: Taker): ZZ32 = t.num(self)
    both(): ZZ32 = sum(self, self)
    listed(): R = self
    bound(): ZZ32 = do
        r: R = self
        r.d
      end
    assigned(): ZZ32 = do
        var r: R = R(0, 0)
        r := self
        r.d
      end
    held(): ZZ32 = Holder(self).r.d
    kept[\T extends Object\](x: T): R = self
    cased(): R = typecase self of
        r: R => self
      end
end

value object R(n: ZZ32, d: ZZ32) extends Q end

den(r: R): ZZ32 = r.d
sum(a: R, b: R): ZZ32 = a.n + b.d

object Taker
    num(r: R): ZZ32 = r.n
end

object Holder(r: R) end

trait Shape comprises { Disc, Square }
    area(): ZZ32 = typecase self of
        c: Disc => discArea(c)
        q: Square => squareArea(q)
